analysis.one_liner: Extends federal anti-discrimination and equal pay protections to independent contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee with two cosponsors until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change six federal civil rights and labor laws so that people who work for a company as independent contractors — gig drivers, freelancers, contract workers — count as "employees" when they claim protection against discrimination based on sex, race, age, disability, genetic information, or unequal pay. Today, many of these workers cannot use those laws against the companies they work for because they are not technically employees. The bill was referred to a House committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent contractors — gig drivers, freelancers, and other contract workers — who today generally cannot sue under federal anti-discrimination or equal pay laws, and workers who may take contract work in the future. A woman paid less than a man for the same contract work, a contractor facing age or disability discrimination, or a worker subjected to harassment would gain a federal legal remedy they currently lack.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds independent contractors to the definitions of "employee" in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (sex, race, religion, national origin discrimination), the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act.
It amends the Fair Labor Standards Act's equal pay provision so that a man and a woman doing comparable contract work for the same employer must be paid the same.

An independent contractor could bring the same kind of federal discrimination lawsuit an employee can, rather than having no federal claim for discrimination committed by the company contracting their services.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely heavily on independent contractors — including gig-economy platforms and businesses using contract labor — would face exposure to discrimination and equal pay lawsuits they currently avoid, plus the legal and compliance costs of treating contractors like employees for these purposes. Small businesses that hire contractors would face the same rules, regardless of size.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not distinguish between genuinely self-employed businesses and workers who are employees in all but name; a one-person design studio contracting with a client would be covered the same as a gig driver, imposing new compliance costs on small firms and truly independent businesses.

Despite the bill's title and summary, the amendment to the Fair Labor Standards Act is limited to its equal pay section, so contractors would gain equal pay rights but not, through this bill, general FLSA wage-and-hour protections such as overtime.
Blurring the line between contractors and employees could lead some companies to use fewer contractors or change how they hire, which could reduce flexible work arrangements some contractors value.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit is concrete: federal anti-discrimination and equal pay rights that contractors currently do not have. The cost falls on companies that use contract labor, in the form of lawsuit exposure and compliance costs. The main design weakness is that the bill covers every independent contractor alike, without any test for who is genuinely self-employed versus an employee in disguise, which could sweep in small businesses and true freelancers along with misclassified gig workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill in the House on February 7, 2018, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
Two Democratic House members cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The committee held no hearing or markup, and no further action was ever recorded on the bill; it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on independent contractor labor, including gig-economy platforms, are better off because the bill died: they continue to operate outside the reach of federal anti-discrimination and equal pay laws for their contract workforce. Contract workers gained nothing.

for.name: Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and published introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.

for.name: 2 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only members beyond the sponsor to support it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill's action history ends with the referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats in the entire House backed the bill (the sponsor plus two cosponsors), and no Republican signed on; with such one-sided but thin support, the fight never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: Platforms classify their drivers as independent contractors, so today those drivers generally cannot sue them under federal anti-discrimination or equal pay laws. This bill would have opened them to such lawsuits and required equal pay across contract work.

industries.industry: Businesses using contract and freelance labor
industries.note: Any firm that staffs work with independent contractors would face discrimination and equal pay liability for those workers, including small firms. The cost to them is the legal remedy gained by the workers.
